utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning to the interpreters, to the court stenographers. Since everybody is here, I would like to say good morning to them as well. I would like to give the floor to Mr. Nobilo, once General Marin has been brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can now continue with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have actually reduced the number of our documents and we have actually reached the last one now. After that, we will show the Brigadier some defence exhibits, which still have not been tendered, but which were submitted during earlier cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D409, A for the French version, B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the 29th of January, 1993, from the command of the Operative Zone, Chief of Staff, Franjo Nakic, is writing to all the Brigades of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia and other units, with a combat report on the situation in the zone of responsibility of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade of Busovaca on the 29th of January, 1993. We will not be reading the document because it speaks of the situation on the front, on that day. Just tell me who wrote this document and who signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As can be seen from the document, I cannot exactly recall who drafted the document, but it was signed by the Chief of Staff, Franjo Nakic. This is his signature and it carries the stamp of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Such reports and others like it, whenever the communications were such that we could send reports of this kind, we would send them to the neighbouring Operative Zone to inform them regarding the situation in our Operative Zone where combat activities were under way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall now show the witness several documents that the Defence has already presented in Court. The first one is D73. Exhibit D73. It would be a good idea to put it on the ELMO so that everyone can see it, or the English version on the ELMO and the Croatian to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. He has refreshed my memory. Actually, this is D73, isn't it? Which was not admitted at the time and that is what you wish to do now, to tender it. What is this document? Anyway, we're listening to you, tell us what is this Exhibit D73? Mr. Registrar, you have marked it? Can I make little notes on it? I know the registrar is watching over me just in case. I know he doesn't like me to scribble on it. Anyway, Mr. Nobilo, it is D73, because it was not authenticated by the witness, it was not admitted, so remind us, what this exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The document is very brief. It was issued by Darko Kralijevic, the commander of the Vitezovi unit on the 24th of April, 1993, and it is a certificate confirming that the flat at address Marshal Tito Street, entrance to the second floor is given for temporary use to Jako Krizanac. The former owner of the flat was Faro Ecnicic, obviously a Muslim. The stamp is of the Vitezovi unit and it is written by Colonel Darko Kralijevic. So I should like to ask the Brigadier first whether he has seen this document, where and when? And whether he knows anything about Jako Krizanac, that Kralijevic gave this flat too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document I am holding in my hand and which we are now reviewing is one that I did not see personally, but I do remember that there were such documents and such certificates. And let me remind you of General Blaskic's order that we discussed yesterday, prohibiting occupation of other peoples' flats who were temporarily absent due to the war. I know that there were such instances and such documents were issued by various entities and one of those was the command of the special purpose unit, Vitezovi, for which it had absolutely no competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did such cases prompt Blaskic to issue the order that we referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such cases did, indeed, prompt General Blaskic to issue that order prohibiting the use of the housing stock, that is the flats vacated by people because of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the stamp of the Vitezovi unit. It says at the bottom, "Defence Department, Special Purpose Unit, Vitezovi and Vitez." And above that it says, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." No mention is made there of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When talking about the organisation of forces, I said that the Vitezovi special purpose unit was not within the organisational structure of the Operative Zone, but was organisationally linked to the defence department of Herceg-Bosna. The competence of the Operative Zone commander in relation to this unit was only as far as its operational use was concerned, whereas disciplinarian matters, logistics and other matters were dealt by this unit, directly with the defence department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Counsel, thank you. We shall now move on to another document, D88, which was submitted but not admitted. Let me briefly present that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, yes, Mr. President. This witness said he never saw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't identify it. It is obviously not his document. But it is a type of document that he recognises. I think that identification need not necessarily mean that a person has to have written it. Brigadier, it's a type of document that doesn't surprise you that you consider it to be quite possible, one of a kind, isn't that so, Brigadier? That is what Mr. Nobilo is asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not surprised by this document. As far as I recall, there were such documents. But, personally, I cannot claim that I held this particular document in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, I think there should be no problem. The exhibit is admitted on condition that its weight will be assessed by the Judges and its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is D88. The second document is of the 4th Battalion of the military police, issued on the 27th of January, 1993, the Commander, Basko Ljubicic, is addressing to the military police department in Mostar an extraordinary report. "On the 24th of January, 1993, at 1445 hours on the main road, Kiseljak to Busovaca, at the locality called Kacuni, fire was opened from infantry weapons on members of the military police from Busovaca, Ivica Petrovic. He was killed on that occasion, together with another civilian person who was with him in the car. The fire was opened by Muslim forces and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both persons were mutilated and cut up with knives. On the 25th of January, 1993, the clashes spread to the entire territory of Busovaca municipality. We have information that the deputy Commander of the first company, Zoran Ljubicic, was hurt in conflicts with Muslim extremists. We were unable to transport him to the hospital and it is possible that he has died. Conflicts are continuing." My first question, Brigadier, is whether you have seen this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not, but I do remember the event and the killing of Ivica Petrovic as we were informed about it by a letter from the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this is how the January conflict in Busovaca started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the report from Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca, it is true that this was one of the immediate causes which led to a later escalation of the conflict in Busovaca municipality in January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are tendering this exhibit into evidence because the witness has confirmed the events referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the Prosecutor has the same position on the document as we had with the prior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will admit the document and they will judge its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is D90.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this document a name is written, so please do not read it or mention it and please do not place it on the ELMO because I think it is a Prosecution witness who was protected. In this document, D90, we're only interested in the second page and the signature of Vladimir Santic. Do you recognise that signature at all? Do you know it? That's all. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know Vladimir Santic and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the stamp of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are tendering this exhibit into evidence on the basis of the recognition of the signature and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is D91. The same witness is referred to so we won't be showing it on the ELMO. But we would like to show you the signature and the stamp. D91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Hayman, feels that D90 and D91 should be under seal because they mention a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, the document has the witness's name on it, it's not supposed to be seen by anybody, including the Brigadier, with all due respect, Brigadier. In any event, if you just ask about the signature and take the document back, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to authenticate it. If you accept this document without authentication, we won't show it to the Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you accept it? Anyway, the Judges can't see it for the moment. And anyway, we must try and find a way out of this dilemma. How are you going to have this witness identify this document? Through what? Has the witness seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He hadn't, I think, not yet, but by means of the stamp and the signature. But on the second page of the document, where the signature is, the same name is mentioned again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Brigadier is going to accept that this is the stamp and this is the signature, then we accept that. Then we have no objection to the document. But what we do object to is that the fashion of showing this document without somehow taking some measures not to disclose the name of a protected witness, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think that we cannot accept this objection because it doesn't say anyway that the person mentioned in this document is a protected witness. The Brigadier or anyone else who may be in the public gallery cannot know that this man was here at all as a witness. So we haven't disclosed the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know this exhibit, Mr. Kehoe, is it your exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it is a Defence Exhibit, Mr. President, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but you are saying that this person should be protected, how do you know that? Everyone is talking about somebody who needs to be protected, but nobody seems to have seen his name. Mr. Kehoe, you have called for protection for a person whose name is figuring in this document, are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could go to private session at this point, we could discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please. Let's go into private session. That would be the best solution. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is D93. Could it please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this document was created on the 30th of January and it was signed by Vladimir Santic and it is sent to the head department of the military police and it is a report on military policemen who were killed in the fighting in Busovaca. Tell me, Brigadier, do you recognise Santic's signature and do you perhaps know the persons who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do recognise the signature of Mr. Vladimir Santic, Commander of the company, and the seal is the seal of the 4th unit of the military police. I do not know anyone of the five policemen who are mentioned as killed in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I suggest that this be moved into evidence. The next one is 95?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The same answer of the Judges. Same objection, same response from the Judges, such to the decision on relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is D94. Could it please be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next document is also a report of the military police of January 29th and it is sent to the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia and the report pertains to killings of Croats in Lasva and Dusina. And Zvonko Rajic is mentioned and then under number 1, Marko Rajic, Pero Rajic, Jozo Kegelj, 60-years-old, many names, et cetera, et cetera, fifteen people all together who were killed in this action taken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are civilians in Lasva and Dusina. On the next page there is a seal and somebody's signature. Can you identify this document in terms of its contents, signature and seal or in some combination of those three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on this document I recognise the seal. I do not recognise the signature, but these events that are mentioned in the report, them, I do remember. Under No. 1, No. 1, Zvonko Rajic, as far as I can remember, he was Commander of a company in the settlement of Dusina in the Lasva region. That is what this place is called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the killing of the Kegelj family, was that something that resounded throughout the Lasva River Valley; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, information on these events quickly spread throughout the Lasva River Valley. As far as I can remember, I saw a picture of the bodies of the killed persons. I saw their corpses, I think, in 1993, on a picture. So, practically, this is the first event, the first big killing, slaughter of the population of the Lasva River Valley and it occurred in January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we wish to offer this document into evidence, D94.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges also maintain their position. All right, this is D95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This was D94 and the next one is D95, the next one that we are going to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So D95, this is a report of the Commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police to Tihomir Blaskic in Kiseljak on the 25th of January, 1993, and the report says on the 25th of January, 1993, at 1.00, in the village of Kacuni, in the fighting between the members of the HVO units of Busovaca and the units of the BH army, Ivica Petrovic was killed and one unknown person. Do you remember this event? You have already mentioned this event. Do you recognise the seal or the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the event. I remember the death of Ivica Petrovic and I recognise the seal of the command of the battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Same objection by the Prosecutor, same position by the Judges. That has been admitted, but the Judges reserve the ability to evaluate the relevance of the exhibit. Last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We give up on this document because, perhaps, it has insufficient detail for identification. But, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that the completion of your cross-examination or do you have any further questions to ask before we take our break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender the documents from D198 to D -- if we include the last one also, 409, so from 198 to D409, we tender them all into evidence and in this way, we do conclude our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can request that the admission of these documents be reserved until the end of the examination. Some of these documents, obviously, the witness had never seen before, et cetera and it's difficult at this point to point out exactly which ones they are. So if we could just reserve on the admission until the end of cross-examination, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be a legitimate request, considering the large number of exposed documents and we will look into the question again at the end of the cross-examination. We're going to take a twenty minute break. We've had a long morning. We're going to take our break. Mr. Kehoe, did you want to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like at some point to discuss the issue of cross-examination. I don't know if you want to do it now. We'll take it up after our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we first have to take a break. The interpreters will have had a long morning. I suggest we take a break and that we start again after a good twenty minute pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours for your cross-examination, but perhaps you want to say something first to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you very much. As Your Honours know that we have been sitting through the testimony of Brigadier Marin for some days now and we do have, I believe, in excess of 200 exhibits that we have that has come before the Court. I will say to you, Mr. President, Your Honours, very few of them have been seen by the Office of the Prosecutor prior to this time. I will also note that many of these documents, as Your Honour well knows, are subject to a binding order issued by this Chamber to various entities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and have not been delivered as this Court knows. What the Office of the Prosecutor is requesting and request making this motion pursuant to the Court's powers under Rule 54 and rule 90(G) and Rule 90(F) is a postponement of the cross-examination of this witness until Wednesday morning. This particular witness has given us documents that are extremely dense, extremely complicated. Just a portion of those documents have been read by the Defence as is their privilege and their right. Nevertheless, there are significant amounts of information located in these documents that need to be explored and the fact of the matter, Mr. President and Your Honours, we have not seen these documents. So these particular documents in conjunction with the testimony of a witness that is obviously very significant for the Defence requires time and preparation. Now I will say to you, Mr. President and Your Honours, such time and preparation will be time well spent. Not only for the preparation time, but also it's going to avoid a needless consumption of time, simply because with that additional time, the Office of the Prosecutor, in her preparation, will be able to focus precisely on the documents that need to be addressed and considered during the cross-examination. Suffice to say, Mr. President, Your Honours, the information that we have received is massive, significant and the testimony is to, pardon me, Your Honour, not clear testimony, but it is somewhat dense in the sense that individual lines or individual items of testimony by the witness involve any other number of other items that must be explored on cross-examination. For all those reasons, Mr. President, Your Honours, we would request a continuance of the cross until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to Mr. Hayman, Mr. Kehoe, about how much time do you think you're going to need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is difficult to say, Mr. President. It is difficult to say at this juncture of the 200 documents, which are not going to be discussed by the Prosecutor, and what need to be discussed in detail. I will say that in consultation with Mr. Harmon and Mr. Cayley, there are some of these documents that we will not be discussing at all. Alternatively, there will be some documents that we'll be discussing in depth. It is difficult, Mr. President, and again I hate to be vague, it is difficult to give an accurate estimate of the cross-examination. This particular witness has been on, I believe, four days. Is that correct, Mr. Dubuisson? Four days with the half days, four full days.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you aware that this is now Defence time that we're counting here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am aware of that, and of course the Office of the Prosecutor has no objection in this time not being held against the Defence. The Prosecutor just believes that in order to have a cogent, focused, cross-examination with this amount of detail, and there is a significant amount of detail in these documents, that there has to be additional time focusing on the testimony in conjunction with the stack of documents that we have all received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Hayman, what is your opinion about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we vigorously oppose a delay in the cross-examination and please allow me to say why. First, what is the actual timing of the events with respect to this witness's testimony? The Defence gave notice of his testimony, including a summary of his testimony on the 15th of September. Nine days passed. On the 24th of September he began his testimony. On the 25th he testified for a half day, therefore, the Prosecutor had a half day to review the witness's testimony up to that point. Then they had the weekend, which constituted the 26th of September, the 27th of September and half of Monday, the 28th of September. That was a two and a half day break for them to review the testimony to date and to prepare their cross-examination. The witness then testified on September 29th and for a half day on September 30th. Again, the other half of that day was available for preparation of cross-examination and for review of the documents of which counsel speaks. Yesterday, of course, the witness testified and today briefly this morning. What do we have before us? We have a weekend. We have this afternoon in which we will not, of course, be in session. There is Saturday, there is Sunday, there is Monday morning. That's three full days, quite frankly, before Monday afternoon, the Monday afternoon session comes around, and realistically we have, perhaps, two hours or less left in the day today. So for all practical purposes, the Prosecutor, even if he commences now, does not have to really commence his cross-examination until Monday afternoon, which follows the upcoming three day equivalent break. The point, Your Honours and Mr. President, is that between the day we gave notice, the 15th of September, and next Monday afternoon, 20 days will have passed. Between the first day of his testimony, the 24th of September, and next Monday afternoon, 12 days will have passed, of which 6.5 days the Court was in recess. The Prosecutor has had an extraordinary opportunity, because of the schedule and the weekends that have come along by happenstance with respect to this witness's testimony. The Prosecutor has had an extraordinary opportunity to review the testimony, the transcripts, indeed, the documents, over a lengthy period of testimony. We maintain that they've had a very fair, indeed leisurely, one might even conclude, opportunity to review these documents, which are voluminous, but they are not in the main lengthy documents. They are not lengthy documents. So our point number one is a delay of this nature is not justified because of the passage of time. Point number two, it's not justified because of other facts and circumstances. What has the testimony of the Brigadier involved? It has involved the events at the heart and core of this case. What was the level of command and control within the HVO? What information was available to the accused on the 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th of April? If they're not prepared to cross-examine on those issues, we submit they weren't prepared to bring this case in the first instance. This is the core of the case. Point number three, to grant them this type of delay would result in unequal treatment of the parties. I would point, for example, to the testimony of Mr. Pajic, or Dr. Pajic, in the Prosecutor's case. Through Dr. Pajic, the Prosecutor introduced at least 1.000 pages of numeroulist and other voluminous legislative statute and materials. He testified extensively concerning those materials between the 30th of June and 1st of July, 1997. Cross-examination commenced immediately thereafter, on the 2nd of July, and concluded on the 3rd of July. A second example of what I refer to when I speak of unequal treatment of the parties that would result from granting the Prosecutor's motion are Exhibits 406, 456 and 457 of the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor. I would hold them up, but they're probably too heavy for me to hold up those four volumes of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you talking about the binders? I am not quite following you. Could you show them to me, please? Are you talking about the binders, are you? Yes, I got the answer from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Four volumes, Mr. President. And these, along with the other volumes, are documents which the Prosecutor introduced with no witness whatsoever. There was no right of cross-examination afforded the Defence with respect to these documents. These documents in the main were sourced to the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but since we know that they are principally HVO documents, that doesn't tell us very much. It doesn't help us how the BH government got them. We have no right of cross-examination with respect to these four volumes of thousands of pages. They had twenty days to prepare, twelve days to actually review the testimony and the documents and they're still not satisfied. To grant their motion would result in unequal treatment of the parties which is contrary to basic notions of fairness and equality of arms. There is a third reason that this motion should not be granted, Your Honours and Mr. President, and that is this witness needs to conclude his testimony. Of course the Prosecutor needs to be given fair and ample time to cross-examine, but the witness is under some time pressure to return to duty. He serves in an integrated federal army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he needs to move on. We need to complete his testimony so that he can return to his duties. He cannot stay here in perpetuity. Lastly, point number five, there would be prejudice to the Defence from granting this motion. I have already described the unequal treatment that would result. We've already given notice of an additional witness that would testify, we thought next week. Obviously, that witness won't testify next week if the cross-examination is delayed. Delay in and of itself is, we believe, unfair. Let none of us forget, of course, that the accused here is in custody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the last point, we have not received any notice on any witness for next week. We have not gotten any notice. Let me talk about a couple of items that were raised by counsel. The first is this long period of time that the Prosecutor allegedly has had to examine this information, given notice of this particular witness. I invite the Court to look back at the factual summary that was given to the Prosecutor by the Defence and compare that particular document to the information that this particular witness has testified about. I think that that will suffice by a pure examination of that one-page document as to what this witness has set forth. What is not in there is astonishing, but I invite the Court to look at it. The second item, with regard to unequal treatment; at the very outset of this case, because of a letter on Mr. Donja and Mr. Dornja, the witness postponed his cross-examination for two weeks because he maintained it wasn't the right name. Let's discuss Major Bower, where the Defence had the opportunity to delay because he didn't want to finish his cross from between the 5th of June and the 29th of June. And to compare this situation with Professor Pajic is not accurate. Professor Pajic was talking about public documents in the public record. They were the Narodni lifts. They were laws on the books of the Croatian community and then the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. We have just gotten in excess of two hundred and some odd exhibits, a handful of which we have seen. And with regard to this leisurely pace, my numbers may be correct, and Mr. Dubuisson, correct me if I'm wrong, but we have received 161 documents since Monday, and most of those documents talking about the fighting that took place in Central Bosnia, are, as counsel points out, at the heart and core of this case. Now, we talk about fundamental fairness, and there is also the fundamental requirement that we attempt to search for the truth through these documents and through this witness's testimony. Heaven knows, the Prosecutor doesn't want to delay this particular witness any more than need be, Mr. President, and Your Honours; however, given the voluminous amount of information this particular witness has presented to this Chamber and to the Prosecutor, and in light of the fact we haven't seen it, adequate preparation time needs to be given to the Office of the Prosecutor, as it was given to the Defence when they requested it, in order to focus this cross-examination on the important issues that the Chamber wants to discuss. Thank you, Mr. President, I don't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, when is Brigadier Marin due to go back to his professional work?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me find out what the latest contact on that was, if I may, Your Honour. My understanding is the fact that he won't be available for at least much of next week is causing some pressure. But we have told him, you know, to expect several days next week, and he has to stay and he has accepted that. But the prospect of the whole week, much less the prospect of spilling over to the next week, is, I think, a difficult one for him. He is in an integrated federal army, and the sooner we can finish and get him back in a normal service of duty situation, the better for his professional and personal situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So I gather we can at least have him next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think, yes. We have told him, and the witness isn't in the room, but this is a public session, perhaps it shouldn't be in public session; suffice it to say, he will remain next week to complete the cross-examination. But if we do not start until Wednesday afternoon, which is a half day, if counsel is committing they will finish between Wednesday afternoon and Friday noon, then that is something different from what they said so far. I don't think they are committing to do that. And I would think that would be a legitimate avenue of inquiry, as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge Riad, in response to that; it depends what this witness has to say. This particular witness was on direct examination for six days. Six days. So, even on the best of circumstances, if we follow the pattern set forth by the Defence, he still wouldn't finish next week. So, using what was given to the Defence during their case of a parody of time between the Prosecutor and the Defence, the Brigadier still wouldn't finish during the six days allocated next week given the fact that under the best of circumstances we only have four, I believe, three or four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, for the sake of argument; since you had six days, if the Prosecution requires six days even next week wouldn't be enough, if we started Monday. Would the witness be able to come back again, as it happens sometimes before?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think to answer that question fully I would need a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you're right about the private session, so we're going to move into private session now. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 21 Whereupon the proceedings adjourned at 12.39 p.m., to be reconvened on 23, the 6th day of October, 1998 at 2.00 p.m. Tuesday
